You don’t have to be super technical to be TPM. 3-4yrs as a IC should be more than enough. It’s more important to show in your resume how your prior experience prep you to be a TPM

I switched from a business analyst / tech product owner role to a tpm. You basically highlight the tpm responsibilities you had while you were in your previous role. A tpm has broad responsibilities like enabling cross team collaboration, executing on a roadmap, defining processes - these are skills you may have picked up or exhibited in previous roles that you can highlight while applying for the position.
If you have not, then would make sense to switch internally or even do a stretch project for your team so you can add it to your resume

It’s challenging because those job search portals have some kind of a filter by title - so your resume may automatically get rejected due to not having the title. Try for an internal referral or if you’re doing a stretch project, specify tpm as a title while highlighting that experience.

FB expectations at L6 :

2/ or you could be running a very technically complex project. Think improving efficiency of our ads delivery engine where the most miniscule change results in $Mn. 
3/ you are expected to ask the hard questions and push to pivot your team direction based on data. 
4/ you look to create new scope either for the product or the program (that could result in staffing up another eng team including TPMs) . Doing this consistently can get you to L7.

Hey Vedant -- I'd say the end-to-end Google interview process is relatively slow. I interviewed for TPM - Cloud Services. I recruiter found me on linkedin, we started chatting in September, had a chat with a "google champion", then 1 PS, then a virtual onsite. Feedback/outcome of virtual onsite was late november. For my experience, I'd say 75% or so of the questions were hypothetical. Things like, PM google street view, PM global laptop refresh, PM repairing all the damaged roads in your city. On the Googliness side I was asked things like how you resolve conflict, and how you would handle learning about a security vulnerability in a vendors software and your boss told you not to tell them about it. Tech questions were not sys design, but more like talking about concepts such as the differences between redundancy and resiliency, how you would manage user access to an internal app with tens of thousands of users. Also, pick a technical concept you are most familiar with and explain it to a non technical person. My advice would be to have project management principles super ironed out that you can then apply across all those various hypothetical situations.

Hey everyone! I’m Rajeev — a senior software engineer with 12+ years of experience, mostly in frontend (React, Tailwind, Node) and earlier LAMP stack work.

I’m currently looking to transition into a Technical Program Manager (TPM) role ,I’m here to learn from this community — especially around making the switch, growing TPM skills, and understanding what success looks like in this role. Looking forward to connecting with others on the same journey or who’ve been through it!
Why do you want to leave eng and move into tpm?
honestly bored of coding now, specially I am bored of solving the same types of frontend problems..  I do not want to be an IC for too long and want to work with cross functional teams!

@jeevs do you mean that you specifically don't want to be an SDE IC for too long? Because if you're making the jump to TPM IC, you'll be an IC for quite some time. Honestly, it sounds like you can solve your problems all within the engineering ladders. If you want to work cross-functionally, you absolutely can do that as an SDE. If you don't want to be an IC, you can absolutely do that as an SDM. If you're bored of FE problems, there are a whole host of other eng problems to solve. 

Honestly, I feel like as a TPM I also end up solving the same set of problems everywhere. Monolithic architectures that no one wants to actually fund splitting up. Site down incidents that don't get proper post-mortem reviews and tangible action taken to reduce. Teams with too many WIP projects instead of doubling down on a handful of problems to make meaningful progress on

@LeverageCoach Wow, thanks for the thoughtful insight — I really appreciate your perspective (definitely made me re-evaluate a few things 😄), especially from someone who’s seen the TPM side in depth.

You’re spot on — there are definitely cross-functional problems and leadership opportunities within the engineering ladder, and I’ve explored a lot of those. Over the years, I’ve taken on work beyond just writing code (as a founding engineer at a startup): leading delivery, aligning with product/backend, breaking down features, and stepping in when UX or backend context was missing. That part of the work interests me more than solving another UI state or debugging CSS quirks now. But at my current workplace, there’s no real path to grow into that kind of role formally.

So it’s less about “getting out of frontend” and more about shifting into a role where my impact is centered around alignment, clarity, and delivery — things I naturally lean into. TPM feels like the right move right now — not just to avoid something, but to move toward what I genuinely enjoy doing.

And yeah, I totally get what you mean about TPMs running into the same systemic issues again and again — not gonna lie, it’s probably no different where I am 😅 but maybe I’m just more excited by a different flavor of recurring problems.

Would love to know how you personally keep the work meaningful in TPM roles? — especially when the challenges start feeling familiar.

@LeverageCoach thanks for sharing your personal take on keeping the work meaningful. and totally agree on idea of finding meaning in the mission of the company,  I’m in a similar phase with a 2-year-old myself. 😄
have you explored the EM role? "alignment, clarity, and delivery" are parts of that job family also.
you have been an eng for 12 years - that's a class 1 citizen in any company. how would you feel about being in a class 2/3 role as a TPM ?
@AG - are there any channels specific for EM roles , didn’t see any in specific

Started a thread.

Hey @AG and others, why class 2/3 citizen in an org? would like to know reason why TPM folks are treated that way? Based on the TPMs I’ve spoken to — and from what I’ve seen on LinkedIn, especially at FAANG companies — most of them have a solid tech background, typically with 7 to 10 years in hands-on coding or SDE roles before transitioning into TPM positions. What I have seen in Bangalore where i work currently its full of engineers and i see there is probably more respect for doers/builders(Eng & Prod) but never seen Project/Program folks getting any less. 

This really made me think and research a lot more about the the role. few question for folks here?
1) Do TPMs get blame for late delivery from Eng or Prod teams?
2) is this role still evolving in some way? I mean now folks with more technical knowledge are preferred in this roles?

Lets answer your qs
1. Yes absolutely - one throat to choke usually or bearer of bad news. 
2. Its evolving in some way with tools that some of the grunt work is going away but yes more technical knowledge folks are preferred

The problem with TPM role is perception and decision making 
1. TPM role is considered mostly overhead (reporting, tracking, unblocking, escalating etc) vs Engineering who are responsible for the delivery of new features/functions etc vs Product/Sales responsible for revenue, 
2. TPM is always stuck between these job profiles. 
3. Reporting structure of a TPM to one of these job profiles then creates a conflict on interest 
my 0.02$

At every company I have been the definition of "TPM" is various so much other than the core of managing projects. Some companies they do more financial / budget related, some is more portfolio related, some more technical, and most (in my exp) not technical at all and mostly take notes and set up meetings

there are some good answers here already.. will add some of my perspectives : 
1/ it is not that the TPM gets blamed for late delivery (tho it looks like many people here have that experience) ; my pet peeve is that TPM is not usually in the room on critical decision making forums. Sure there are folks here who have gained so much respect that they are invited - but that is the exception and not the norm. 
2/ @terry. answers the evolution question well - it is not so much that the role is evolving - more so that there's no standard definition of what a TPM does. Most of the other critical product building functions (prod, eng, design, data) don't have that confusion AFAICT. Also, most people in these roles don't fall into these tracks "by accident"- Eng go to school for it. PM is extremely coveted and people bend over backwards to get that role.. people with aesthetic taste go into design and folks who like mucking around with data go into DS.. most program/project managers do this job mostly as a happy accident, and stop caring about the craft or getting better at it.. and we've gotten branded as the nagging people who follow up constantly without providing any value 🤷🏻 

PS: this maybe a very cynical view, but these days when all roles are morphing to new forms in the AI age, you want to go down a new career path very thoughtfully and eyes wide open. It does seem from your answers that you care about the craft in general, which might be one of the best reasons to actually go down this path. Don't go down this path because "you hate engineering" or "coding isn't your jam" - but do it truly if you have fell in love with the craft 🙂
